## TL;DR

Made the existing `PageSkeleton` timing gate the default for every skeleton instance. That applies the shared 180 ms show delay and 350 ms minimum-visible interval to Checks, Agents, Releases, Deployments, Dev, Secrets, Settings, and the other panels that use the same component. Views keep their existing loading conditions and layouts; no view contains its own timer. The component continues using the shared activity-motion controller and reduced-motion preference. Added default-behavior fake-timer coverage and updated loading tests to wait for the shared gate. The scoped RepoOS check passed.

## Work and rationale

The shell-level skeleton already used the right mechanism: `PageSkeleton` accepted `defer`, and its deferred branch already canceled a pending show when loading finished quickly, held a visible skeleton until its minimum interval elapsed, and emitted visibility changes for the shell. The inconsistency came from the component defaulting `defer` to false. Every view-level callsite passed a loading condition but omitted the opt-in flag, so those instances rendered immediately and could disappear almost at once.

I changed the component default to enable the gate. Keeping the behavior in the shared component means each view remains responsible only for saying whether its data is loading. The view list in the task, along with shared panels such as Check Runs, reminders, scheduled tasks, and model providers, now receives identical timing behavior without duplicate state or timers. The shell’s explicit `defer` remains valid and documents its intent. This also covers the secondary Releases distribution skeleton, which shares the component but has its own loading condition.

The cache behavior follows from the existing page-data flow. `refreshPageData` delivers a fresh in-memory cached value synchronously before the background request settles. Those receive callbacks update the view state and clear the loading condition in the same turn; with a delayed skeleton, a cache hit cancels the timer before anything is rendered. Secrets already had cache-seeded state, and the other page caches now benefit from the shared gate on their revisits without adding view-specific cache checks. A genuinely uncached slow request still displays a skeleton after the delay and keeps it visible for the minimum interval.

The component continues to use `useActivityMotion`, which coordinates animation concurrency and visibility, and it keeps the existing reduced-motion class and transition behavior. The skeleton markup and layout dimensions stay in place, so replacing it with content does not require a new layout strategy. The tests now exercise the default component behavior with fake timers: the skeleton is absent before the delay, appears at the delay, remains while the minimum interval is outstanding, then disappears. The existing cached-load test covers a value that clears loading before the delay.

I updated tests that asserted immediate per-view visibility to advance their fake timers or wait past the shared delay. Tests for cached revisits continue to assert that no skeleton is shown. For Secrets, the pending uncached state explicitly advances through the minimum-visible interval before asserting the skeleton has left after the resource resolves.

## Approaches tried

I first considered adding `defer` to every listed view template. That would make the UI behave correctly, but it would preserve an easy way for a future `PageSkeleton` callsite to accidentally opt out, and it would spread a behavior the task specifically asks to implement once. Making the shared component’s default deferred was the smaller and more durable change. No composable was necessary because the component already owned the timer lifecycle, visibility event, reduced-motion state, and motion coordination.

I also checked whether cache seed logic needed to be duplicated into each view. The shared page cache already synchronously invokes the subscriber with fresh cached data. The default delay naturally suppresses that transient loading state, so adding `getCachedPageData` calls to several views would duplicate cache details without improving what the user sees.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check found tests that assumed a skeleton existed immediately. I updated those assertions to wait for the configured delay. A later run exposed test harness issues caused by advancing timers in a cached-data test and leaving fake timers active in a test that also waits on a real zero-delay timeout. I moved timer advances to the true first-load cases, used real elapsed time where the view test helper itself depends on real timers, and restored fake timers explicitly in cleanup where required.

The remote validation host hung during two attempts and RepoOS retried on another host. The eventual remote run passed. That successful run completed the UI build and 512 scoped test cases; local format, lint, build, contrast, branch-artifact, and UI smoke guards also passed. No human input or external service action was required.

## Key learnings

A shared component can already contain the complete behavior and still fail to be shared in practice if the safe behavior is opt-in. Defaults matter: making the delayed path the default protects future callsites while leaving each view’s loading predicate simple.

A short show delay also acts as a cache-hit policy. When cached state is delivered synchronously, the pending timer is canceled before the user sees a placeholder. This provides consistent revisit behavior through the existing cache contract rather than relying on parallel per-view initialization logic.

Tests for delayed UI should distinguish three conditions: before the delay, after the delay while still loading, and after loading ends but before the minimum visible duration expires. Tests that share fake timers with helpers using real timers need to account for that boundary and restore timer mode so later cases do not inherit a frozen clock.
